Describe the change you are proposing.
We propose to implement the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They unite students and instructors to enhance non- honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC - see: https://www.nchchonors.org/directors-faculty/definition-of-honors-education).

Honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials (not just more.) Contracts would be approved by the Honors Program and— before approving honors credit for the course –the outcomes would also be assessed by the Honors Program in collaboration with the faculty, via the contracted rubric. Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.

Considering the Honors Contract as an Effective Tool for Furthering Honors Education at URI SUMMARY This document briefly explores the concept of honors contracts, formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, uniting students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an hon- ors level through additional work tailored to the “broader, deeper and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC).
Contracts are recog- nized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership, enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
Successful honors contracts depend on effective setup, management, and assessment at the hon- ors administration level.
Customization to students’ and faculty interests is essential, providing personalized educational journeys and one-on-one time with instructors.
Students looking to set up contracts should follow a structured approach, guided by honors administration.

This could include early communication about opportunities, advising to educate students on the process and benefits, and encouraging them to approach advisors when identify- ing contract possibilities.
Initiating the process involves engaging with faculty, guided by advis- ing, before registration.
Detailed contracts specifying the project, its outcomes, deadlines, and contact schedules, ensure clarity.
Faculty handle grading, with the honors organization approving credits.
Contracts should bridge the gap between honors and non-honors classrooms, maintaining high standards and clear expectations.
To ensure the effectiveness of honors contracts, too routine or casual use must be prevented.
They should complement, not replace, the program’s curriculum, while preserving community and support.
Faculty involvement should be incentivized and re- warded to maintain a dynamic and successful contract system.

Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals and allow programs to meet student needs when constraints of students or faculty numbers or funding limitations do not allow honors courses to be run that answer to their interests and needs.
This empowers students, fosters motivation, and facilitates mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. ~KA NOTES ON HONORS CONTRACTS KARL ASPELUND, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, URI HONORS OCTOBER 23, 2023

WHAT IS AN HONORS CONTRACT?
AN HONORS CONTRACT is a signed agreement between a student and in- structor.
Facilitated by the honors program, the contract states that the student will complete a specified project in addition to other coursework required and thus “convert” the non-honors class to an honors-equivalent course through additional work, such as outside reading, independent research, or some other enhanced learning activity (Badenhausen, 7).
Usually, students are required to earn both an A or B grade for the regular coursework and submit acceptable contract work to qualify for honors credit. (James, 30) A little over 60% of honors programs in the USA—regardless of institutional type—use contracts (Bahls, 172.) CONTRACTS provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough of a student body to fill hon- ors sections.
Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for students’ self-guided intellectual growth (Bahls, 175).

For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kan- sas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.
They can “facilitate access to honors, increase completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with struc- tured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences” (Dotter, 56).
Honors contracts not only maximize faculty-student contact in classes of any format, they also accommodate exploration and questioning in a range of research disciplines, from team-taught humanities discussions to innovative in- vestigations in STEM courses, including their labs (Myers and Whitebread, 22.) Further, as a valued part of honors education, tutorial-based contracts can be seen as a special approach used in various modes of learning: Research and creative scholarship, breadth and enduring questions, service learning and leadership, experiential learning, and learning communities.

They can therefore similarly result in the “broader, deeper, and more complex learning-centered and learner-directed experiences” with which the NCHC defines honors educa- tion (Myers and Whitebread, 40 & NCHC Shared Principles and Practices).
WHY USE HONORS CONTRACTS?
Provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility Empower students to their own learning experiences Maximize faculty-student contact Result in broader, deeper, and more complex learning centered and learner direct- ed experiences An agreement, mediated by the honors program, be- tween student and instructor that defines further work that“converts” the non-hon- ors class to an honors equivalent course. 60+ % of programs use contracts 2 Honors education is characterized by in-class and extracurricular activities that are measurably broader, deeper, or more complex than comparable learn - ing experiences typically found at institutions of higher education.

Honors expe - riences include a distinctive learner-directed environment and philosophy, pro - vide opportunities that are appropriately tailored to fit the institution’ s culture and mission, and frequently occur within a close community of students and faculty. ~National Collegiate Honors Council: Definition of Honors Education

HOW ARE CONTRACTS SET UP EFFECTIVELY?
A COMPREHENSIVE SET OF GUIDELINES, that include the basic expecta- tions of the honors experience and specific expectations for contracting, should be available and presented to students early on.
These should include that two of the primary purposes of contracting are to: 1) enable a student and faculty member to establish a one-to-one, ongoing mentor-mentee relationship through- out the semester and 2) to enable the student to experience the subject matter in more depth. (Bolsch, 54) Three honors-related dissertations reporting mixed experiences with contracts find or imply that students appreciate contracts when they meet two conditions: 1) student and faculty customize the work to fit a student’s interests, and 2) con- tracts involve significant time with the instructor (Myers and Whitebread: 23) Faculty members should be solely responsible for assigning course grades.
However, the contracting process should be structured from the outset as one in which the honors organization certifies that a successfully contracted course should be designated for “honors credit” on a student’s transcript.

So, while the faculty member assigns the grade for the course based on requirements unrelat- ed to the contract, honors administration is responsible for placing, essentially, a “seal of approval” on each contract experience through an additional transcript notation once it receives the faculty member’s certification that the elements of the contract were completed. (See: Bolsch, 52) Creating databases for honors advisors of all past digital contracts, searchable by course and faculty mentor’s name can lead to more proactive advising about innovative approaches to contracts and increased access to examples before students even meet with faculty. (Thomas & Hunter, 242) THE A V AILABILITY AND BENEFITS OF CONTRACTS need to be careful- ly publicized to newly-arrived honors students.
Honors advisors should initially help students understand where in their trajec- tory an honors contract might be instrumental and beneficial.
It should be made clear how important a dialogue with instructors will be, and how much this relies on student initiative and their own vision for their learning.

Honors administration and advisors should promote that students, immediate- ly on identifying a course within which they´d be interested to do contracted work, that they talk with an honors advisor to ensure that they understand the process and are aware of their options. “These meetings allow students to re- hearse future conversations with faculty in a safe environment, enable advisors to set clear expectations for contracts, and equip students with the necessary language to meet those expectations” (Dotter, 59.) Students should approach instructors before registering to discuss options and get a firm commitment so the contract is viable and that the honors credits they are receiving that term will be sufficient for their continuing success.
HOW SHOULD STUDENTS APPROACH SETTING UP A CONTRACT?
Searchable databases of past digital contracts lead to more proactive advising Publicize contracts early and often!
Encourage students to ap- proach advisors as soon as they see an opportunity for a contract arise.

Students must approach faculty—with the help of ad- vising— before registering to begin the process Two primary purposes: Enabling a mentor-mentee relationship and a more in-depth experience of the subject matter Students appreciate con- tracts that are fitted to their interests and afford signifi- cant time with the instructor Faculty assign grades, the honors organization ap- proves the honors credits and notifies Enrollment Services.
Advise students early on about the process and bene- fits of contracts 3
WHAT MIGHT A CONTRACT STIPULATE?

FIVE COMPONENTS should be, at least, required for a contract: 1) A substantial (15-20 p.) paper or project (of equivalent time/effort: c. 20 hours) should be defined and outlined. 2) It should be required that the student share the knowledge/skills/experienc- es gained through the paper or project with an audience, either in the class or elsewhere. 3) The contract should include a plan for how the faculty member and student have regular contact outside of class to discuss the student’s progress and an- swer questions regarding the paper or project. 4)The student should be required to state specifically on the contract form how they will meet each of the three NCHC requirements of “broader, deeper, more complex.” 5) A date at the midpoint of the semester should be determined at which the faculty member should provide a brief report to honors administration on the contact they have had with the student and assess the student’s progress to date. (See: Bolsch 2005: 55) CONTRACTS EXEMPLIFY THE BEST OF HONORS PEDAGOGY when, anchored in the tutorial model, they cultivate personalized, mentored learning and ensure consistent, documented quality (Myers and Whitebread, 22).

It is therefore important that honors administrators and advisors keep a close eye on the contracts created, their implementation, and progress, and provide solid templates and rubrics for their creation and use.
While contract courses do not always provide a venue for honors students to interact with each other, they do create space for students to collaborate with instructors and develop important mentoring relationships (Wyatt, 215).
This outcome–a “win-win” if well managed–must be continually emphasized to both faculty and students.
An inclusive pedagogical practice opens the curriculum to a wide array of fac- ulty who become stakeholders in honors.
It has been shown that these curricular practices have led to greater acceptance of and appreciation for honors colleges on campuses where faculty participation is widespread (Wyatt, 196).
Honors administration must therefore constantly work toward an awareness of these practices among all faculty at the University, whether they teach honors students or not.
WHAT ARE EXAMPLES OF POSITIVE OUT- COMES FROM THE USE OF CONTRACTS?

Contracts must be well managed and assessed at the honors admin. level so that they be the effective tool that they are.
Contracts foster and sup- port a sense of community and ownership around hon- ors programs.
The contract should define the contracted project, its deliverables and intended outcomes and deadlines, as well as points of contact and required feedback by the faculty supervisor.
Maintain the awareness that contracts are a venue for meaningful student-faculty relationships. 4

WHAT ARE EXAMPLES OF POSSIBLE PROBLEMS THAT APPEAR WHEN USING CONTRACTS AND WHAT ARE PATHS TOW ARD AVOIDING THEM?
PROBLEMS THAT APPEAR ARE NOT INSURMOUNTABLE.
Mostly they are cir- cumvented by a continuing awareness of processes and a care for good structures and assessment, creating contracts that enhance rather than concede the honors experience (Bambina, 122).
Contracts must not become “routine” or commonplace, no matter what their number.
Nor can they become a “secret fix” only available to those “in the know.” The narrow definition of honors programs can lead to charges of elitism and segre- gation if honors students, who increasingly tend to be upper-middle-class, white, and female, become insulated from the general student population in an honors curricular bubble.
The contract approach mitigates this by allowing students to learn in an in- clusive campus-wide environment while still engaging in an honors curriculum and community (Wyatt, 196).
Overworked instructors may agree to contracts but then require little more than comple- tion of extra assignments with minimal instructor-student interaction.

Honors educators have the responsibility to eliminate underdeveloped honors contracts that dilute rather than enrich the academic experiences of students. (Wyatt, 195.) It is good practice for evaluation and assessment templates to be created and provided by the honors organiza- tion.
And oversight of contracts by honors administrators must therefore be well-struc- tured, mandated, and clear, and guidelines must be provided to faculty on deadlines and assessment rubrics.
It is essential that contracted work not simply be “more”; rather, it must be meaningful- ly integrated in each case with the course content and learning goals and the work the course already requires. (Bahls, 177) The contract must therefore measurably outline work that leads to the “broader, deeper, and more complex learning-centered and learn- er-directed experiences” with which the NCHC defines honors education (NCHC).

The suggestion that the learning experience of a contracted class is equivalent to a stand-alone honors class—seeing as the student receives academic credit for both— opens honors programs and colleges up to potential exploitation by administrators who may not see the need for assigning appropriate resources to honors or may even try to cut budgets. (Badenhausen, 11) It must therefore be agreed—and practiced—that when options are limited, contracts are a workable path to honors completion that benefits both the students and the institution, not a work-around for the program or institution to avoid curriculum development and creating classes.
But even though the close community of students and faculty that defines honors edu- cation is achieved here by other means, the importance of achieving a sense of belong- ing to the larger cohort should not be ignored.
Therefore, a stricture should be in place that students be limited in the number of credits they can complete through contracts, especially in their freshman and sophomore years.

Finally, with increasing demands and tightening budgets overburdening faculty with unpaid work that is not recognized in reviews, it is essential that faculty be recognized and compensated for the additional work a contract entails.
Otherwise, faculty fatigue may set in and departments and colleges may resent the outside burdens (Bambina, 118).
The equivalent of a one-credit independent study would seem reasonable, and perhaps an amendment to faculty contracts might state the value of this work for pro- motion and tenure reviews.
Contracts bring honors students into non-honors classrooms, mitigating the separation of honors stu- dents from others.
Contracts are a beneficial part of the honors methods in individual cases, not a substitute for the program.
Students should be a part of an honors cohort, con- tacts should not be allowed to separate them from the group.
Administration must take care to never let contracts become routine or a “secret fix.” Honors admin. must work diligently to maintain high standards, and clear expec- tations Contract-work must mea- surably achieve NCHC goals: broader, deeper, and more complex learning experiences.
Faculty must be rewarded for the work they do, lest fatigue or resentment under- mine the contract system. 5

Faculty Senate Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Report #2001-02-1 November 19, 2001 As approved by the Faculty Senate on December 13, 2001 Amendments to the Constitution of the Faculty Senate Recent changes of titles and/or responsibilities of administration officials have affected certain ex officio members of the Faculty Senate listed in the membership paragraph (Article III) of the Faculty Senate Constitution. The Faculty Senate Executive Committee has asked the CBUM Committee to consider the constitution's membership article in light of these changes. At a meeting on November 7, 2001, the consensus of the CBUM Committee members was that no changes to the Senate Constitution are to be made without a referendum as provided for in Article VII of the Faculty Senate Constitution. That constitution, stating the Senate's fundamental principles, is too important a document to permit its being changed editorially; among other things because there may be disagreement on whether a change is editorial or substantive. This implies that changes to the titles and/or responsibilities of members of the administration who are also ex officio members of the Faculty Senate ought not to occur by administrative fiat, but are to be preceded by consultation with the body whose constitution they affect. Nevertheless, the CBUM Committee's consensus was that the following Senate Constitution changes required to make the document consistent with recent administrative action are comparatively non-controversial: From Vice Provost for Academic Programs and Services to Vice Provost for Academic Affairs. CBUM #1 http://www.uri.edu/facsen/CBUM 01-02-1.html 1 of 5 1/23/14, 1:59 PM

From Vice Provost for Research and Service to Vice Provost for Graduate Studies, Research and Outreach. From Vice President for Student Development to Vice President for Student Affairs. From Vice President for University Relations to Vice President for University Advancement. From Dean of Admissions and Financial Aid to Dean of Admissions. Accordingly, the CBUM Committee recommends that the Senate approve a future referendum authorizing those changes to the Senate Constitution. There are, however, also some changes that were deemed to be rather substantive. They are: The abolition of the Dean of the College of Continuing Education and concurrent institution of the position of Vice Provost for Urban Programs. The abolition of the Dean of the Graduate School and subsuming that official's responsibilities under those of the Vice Provost for Graduate Studies, Research and Outreach. The abolition of the position of Registrar and subsuming that official's responsibilities under the newly created position of Director of Enrollment Services. (Note that the Registrar, whose position is to be merged with that of another official who is as of now not even an ex officio member of the Senate, is a Faculty Senate Officer whose duties CBUM #1 http://www.uri.edu/facsen/CBUM 01-02-1.html 2 of 5 1/23/14, 1:59 PM

include an important function in conducting referendums.) Therefore, the CBUM Committee has decided to invite on the Senate floor an open discussion of these three substantive position changes, and to use the input of that discussion, possibly even including motions containing instructions to the committee, to frame recommendations with respect to future referendums on these matters.
It is hoped that the URI administration will, as a part of that discussion, provide its rationale and justification for the changes in administrative positions involved.
The committee also recommends that the constitutional amendments on the matters designated above as editorial be conducted only after the other matters have been disposed of in order that referendums possibly resulting from that disposition can be conducted simultaneously with the referendums recommended in this report.

GEC End-of-Year Report for the May 7, 2026, Faculty Senate Meeting
General Education Assessment: C2 and D1 Outcomes
This is a summary of the key findings and recommendations from the General Education assessment, focusing on the C2—Global Responsibilities—and D1—Integrate and Apply—outcomes.
Starting with C2: the expectation is that all students reach competency by graduation. The outcome is designed to position students within a global framework by asking them to engage with histories, cultures, institutions, and languages, and to move beyond understanding toward identifying and analyzing responsible action in response to complex global issues. In principle, it’s one of the most ambitious components of the GenEd program: it aims to cultivate knowledge and foster a sense of ethical responsibility and purpose within an interconnected world. Among the most urgent findings, which is echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proficiency in a language other than English among our students. This isn’t a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

What we see in the data is partial progress toward that goal. Most students place at the level of approaching competency, with stronger performance in applying regional knowledge, understanding global systems, and reflecting on their own cultural perspective. These are important strengths that suggest our curriculum is building foundational global awareness effectively.
However, there are consistent gaps. Students struggle most with communicating in a language other than English, considering multiple perspectives, and—most notably—examining global responsibilities. Even at the upper levels, where we see developmental gains, these areas remain underdeveloped. The data suggest that students are better at knowing than at doing—that is, they can describe global issues but are less prepared to engage them critically or propose solutions.
We also note a structural limitation: only about 37% of courses participated in the C2 assessment. That level of participation constrains how broadly we can generalize these findings.

Turning to D1: this outcome is intended to move students beyond disciplinary silos by emphasizing the interconnectedness of knowledge and its application to complex, real-world problems. Positioned primarily at the 300- and 400-level, it assumes that students will draw on prior learning across the GenEd curriculum to synthesize ideas, transfer skills, and respond effectively to new academic and professional challenges. In this sense, D1 represents the culminating logic of GenEds: not just the accumulation of knowledge, but its integration and use.
Here the results are stronger. Students most often meet or approach competency, particularly in transferring skills, connecting knowledge, and engaging in integrative learning. This is encouraging and suggests that, where integration is explicitly built into coursework, students perform well.

That said, the D1 data come with even more significant limitations. Only 13% of courses participated, and the sample is heavily weighted toward upper-division courses, limiting representation of earlier stages in the undergraduate experience and our ability to assess developmental progression. So, while the results are positive, they are not yet comprehensive.
Across both outcomes, student performance is closely tied to assignment design. Where assignments are well aligned with GenEd outcomes, students demonstrate competency. Where that alignment is unclear—or where assignments do not explicitly ask for reflection, perspective-taking, or application—student performance drops accordingly.
So, what’s next?
* First, GEC recommends clearer and more explicit guidelines for aligning assignments with GenEd outcomes, particularly in Kuali submissions.
* Second, we recommend investment in faculty development—workshops and resources that help instructors design assignments that elicit the kinds of learning we are trying to measure.

* Third, and critically, we need to find a way to increase faculty participation in assessment. Without broader participation, we risk turning assessment into a compliance exercise rather than a meaningful tool for program improvement.
* Finally, we recommend that certain criteria be revisited—especially––and I emphasize this: language use within C2, to see how criteria are defined and implemented across disciplines, to ensure they are both rigorous and applicable.
A Key Emerging Concern: Language Proficiency
Among the most urgent findings echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proficiency in a language other than English among our students. This isn't a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

At a time when we position global competency, intercultural awareness, and cross-cultural communication as central institutional goals, the fact that relatively few students graduate with functional proficiency in another language reveals a misalignment between our stated outcomes and our curricular realities. We're asking students to demonstrate global understanding without consistently providing them the most fundamental tool required to achieve it.
This raises a set of unavoidable questions for the committee and for the university: What is the role of language study within General Education? And more importantly, can we credibly claim to prepare students for global citizenship and an increasingly multilingual workforce if language proficiency remains peripheral to the curriculum?

Without sustained and meaningful engagement in language learning, our claims of intercultural competence risk remaining aspirational rather than demonstrable. If C2 is to function as more than a conceptual framework, then we need to treat language proficiency as a central pathway to achieving its goals, not as an optional enrichment. Despite our stated goals of fostering global understanding and communication across cultures, relatively few students graduate with functional proficiency in another language. This disconnect raises fundamental questions about:
* The role of language study within our GenEd requirements
* Whether GenEd is adequately preparing students for global citizenship and workforce demands
In short, the program is working, but unevenly. Students are learning, but not always in the ways we intend to measure. With stronger alignment, clearer expectations, and broader participation, we can close that gap.

1 University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees Regulations Regarding Use of University Property [DRAFT 20241008 CC] Introduction As noted in the University of Rhode Island’s Mission Statement and consistent with University values, the University of Rhode (also “University” or “URI”) is committed to high- quality education, community engagement, and the freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good.
The management of University Property and other resources is paramount to meeting that mission.
Authority and Applicability Pursuant to Rhode Island General Laws §§ 16-32-2 and 16 -32-2.1, the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees is empowered to make rules and regulations for the control and use of Univ ersity Property while the President of the University is responsible for the general management of University Property.

These regulations apply to all users of University Property , including all members of the University community (students, faculty, staff, and affiliates) and third parties (individuals, groups, and members of the public) who wish to use any University Property for any purpose.
Definitions University Operations.
All teaching , research, community engagement, and business functions, as well as any other official activity of the University.
University Property.
Property belonging to the State of Rhode Island and held in trust by the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees; property held by the University of Rhode Island or any of its component units in its own name; and property owned by third parties but assigned to, occupied by, or managed by the University or any of its component units.
University Property includes all real property, including without limitation land, buildings and other structures, fences, driveways and walkways, and other permanent improvements and associated infrastructure .
For the purposes of these regulations, property leased or licensed to a third party is excluded from the definition of University Property. 1.

General The primary purpose of University Property is to support the University’s mission.
Every individual and group using University Property is expected to use it in a manner that (i) complies with all applicable laws, policies, procedures, rules, and regulations; (ii) is safe and responsible; (iii) maintains and protects the integrity, cleanliness, and functionality of the University Property; (iv) does not materially and substantially disrupt or interfere with University Operations; and (v) does not impinge upon the individual rights of another person or group.

2 Access to and use of University Property is governed by the University, not by colleges, departments, or administrative units.
Individual colleges, departments, and administrative units may adopt guidelines governing the use of University Property allocated for their specific use provided that such guidelines are consistent with these regulations.
Space is allocated pursuant to the University’s policy on Allocation and Utilization of Space. 2.
Limitations and Prohibited Activities The University may establish reasonable standards and limitations regarding the time, place, and manner of use for any University Property, including access to certain areas within a building, entire buildings themselves, or specified areas of University Property, by both the general public and the University community.
The University also has the right to restrict access t o any and all University Property, including the campus(es) as a whole, as necessary to address safety and/or security concerns.

Specific requirements relative to the limitations and prohibited activities (e.g., building hours, decibel levels, posting, etc.) may be developed by the Department of Public Safety and posted on the Public Safety website. a.
Individual Rights : Under no circumstances may University Property be used in a manner that impinges upon the rights of another person under the United States or Rhode Island Constitution; any federal, state, or local law; or any University policy. b.
Violation of Law: Any use of University Property that violates federal, state, or local laws, regulations, or ordinances will constitute a violation of these regulations. c.
Disruption of University Operations : The use of University Property must not materially and substantially disr upt or interfere with the conduct of University Operations or scheduled meetings, programs, or events. d.
Campus and Building Access and Egress : Any use of University Property must not impede access to, use of, or egress from University Property (or otherwise impede access to or egress from sanctioned University functions and activities) or impede vehicular or pedestrian right-of-way.

Driving on walkways or accessing gated roadways unless authorized or otherwise posted is strictly prohibited. e.
Endangerment: The use of University Property may not be used in a manner that endangers others or is violent or incites violence. f.
Leafletting and Distribution of Literature : Leafletting or the distribution of literature is allowed provided that the activity does not impede the flow of pedestrian or vehicular traffic, block access or egress, or create litter; and the item is not placed on motor vehicles or forced upon others.
Housing and Residential Life and Dining Services may develop additional restrictions on leafletting specific to areas under their control. g.
Signs, Postings, Banners : Posting of information is limited to designated bulletin boards or other areas identified for pos ting.
Affixing signs unrelated to University Operations into or on University Property, other than designated areas, is prohibited.
Affixing signs or banners to the exterior of buildings without prior permission from the Offices of the Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs and Provost, Vice

3 President for Student Affairs , or Vice President for Administration and Finance is prohibited.
Except for within designated spaces dedicated to postings and announcements, printed matter such as posters, fliers, and stickers may not be affixed to University Property.
No signs supported by standards or st icks shall be permitted in any assembly inside any building on campus.
Signs supported by standards or sticks shall be permitted outside. h.
Graffiti: Graffiti is defined as u nauthorized and unlawful writings or drawings made on a wall or other surface.
Graffiti is not protected speech, and may be considered the illegal defacement of property, punishable as a crime under Rhode Island General Law (RIGL § 11-44-21.1).
Temporary markings, such as chalking, are permissible provided the speech is lawful and the markings are easily removable. i.
Erection of Structures : No structure, permanent or temporary, may be erected on University Property without the specific written approval of the Vice President for Administration and Finance.

Camping, defined as the erection of a temporary shelter or otherwise maintaining a space designed for living (eating, sleeping, etc.) outside, is prohibited without written permission from the Office of the Vice President for Administration and Finance or the Office of the Vice President for Student Affairs j.
Amplified Sound: Sound level must be maintained at a volume that does not interfere with University Operations; sound emission beyond the perimeters of the reserved area shall be at a reasonable level.
Specific requirements will be developed by the Department of Public Safety and posted to the Department of Public Safety website. k.
Building Access: Access to non-residential buildings shall not be permitted outside of posted hours unless specifically authorized by the responsible depart ment.
Access to residential buildings is by invitation only and the University reserves the right to ask guests to leave at any time. l.
Building Exteriors : Climbing, scaling, or rappelling on University Property is prohibited unless expressly permitted in writing by the Vice President for Administration and Finance or their delegate. m.
Bicycles, Skateboards and S imilar Conveyances.

The use of bicycles, scooters, skateboards, and similar means of motorized and non- motorized conveyance on University property ( except for mobility aids) may be controlled by specific requirements established by the Department of Public Safety. n.
Open Flames and Fire Safety : Any activity that includes the possession or use of fireworks or the use of fire pits, campfires, or torches without prior written permission by the University (and/or local or state fire authorities) are prohibited.
Protected candles (candles with wind screens) may be used with prior approval from the Department of Publ ic Safety.
The unauthorized or improper activation, possession, use, removal, or disabling of fire safety equipment and/or warning devices; failure to follow standard fire safety procedures; and/or interference with firefighting equipment or personnel are prohibited. o.
Sanitation: Urination or defecation in any place other than a designated restroom is prohibited.

4 3.
Enforcement and Violations Violations of this policy may lead to disciplinary actions up to and including termination from employment, suspension or expulsion from the University, revocation of affiliate status, or a permanent restriction or trespass from University Property.
Such discipline for students will be imposed under the Student Handbook and for employees under applicable Human Resourc e Administration policies, collective bargaining agreements, or other controlling agreements.
In addition, the Board of Trustees may impose fines, with a schedule determined by the Department of Public Safety, up to statutory limits plus associated costs pursuant to RIGL § 16-32-2.
Violations of these regulations may lead to removal from University Property, possible loss of further access to and use of University Property, and/or prosecution for trespass, disorderly conduct, or other offenses under state law.
